prompt: Use an ideal lower-bound GEO bent-pipe model: request and reply each traverse ground → satellite → ground, with every leg set to the 35,786 km orbital altitude. At about 299,792 km/s, what propagation RTT does the four-leg model give?

options.explanation: That is a single leg: you to the satellite. The request also has to come back down, and the reply has to make the same trip.
That is the one-way delay (up and down once). A round trip needs the reply to go up and down as well: four legs.
Correct. Four legs of about 35,786 km: 4 × 35,786 / 299,792 ≈ 0.477 s.
20 ms does not follow from the supplied GEO distance. Lower orbits can have much smaller propagation delays, but actual service RTT requires additional path information.

workedExample:
1. The request goes you → satellite → ground station: 2 legs.
2. The reply goes ground station → satellite → you: 2 more legs.

```formula
RTT = 4 × h / c
RTT = 4 × 35,786 km / 299,792 km/s
RTT = 143,144 / 299,792 s ≈ 0.477 s
RTT ≈ 477 ms
where
RTT: the propagation round-trip time
h: the satellite's altitude, 35,786 kilometres (km); each leg is taken as this vertical distance
c: the speed of light in a vacuum, about 299,792 km/s
km/s: kilometres per second
s: second
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: four trips of nearly 36,000 km at light speed take almost half a second.
```

3. In practice you also pay for slant range (you are rarely directly under the satellite), processing and terrestrial backhaul, so actual latency exceeds the idealised vertical-leg component. This does not establish a universal 600 ms service RTT.

prompt: Compare two hypothetical equal-direction paths, ignoring curvature and processing: (a) 17,000 km of fibre, where light travels at its vacuum speed divided by an assumed effective group index of 1.47 (about 204,000 km/s); (b) 550 km up + 17,000 km across space + 550 km down, at the vacuum speed of light, about 299,792 km/s. What are their propagation RTTs?

options.text: Fibre about 167 ms; laser about 121 ms
Both about 113 ms, because light has the same speed in both
options.explanation: Light in glass is slowed by the assumed effective group index (1.47). In vacuum it moves at the full c, which is the whole point of the comparison.

options.text: Fibre about 83 ms; laser about 60 ms
options.explanation: These are one-way delays. A round trip doubles them.

options.text: Laser slower, because the extra 1,100 km up and down outweighs any speed gain
options.explanation: The extra 1,100 km is only about 6% more distance, while vacuum is about 47% faster than glass. The laser path still wins comfortably.

workedExample:
```formula
RTT = (2d) / v
RTT_f = 2 × 17,000 km / 203,940 km/s
RTT_f ≈ 0.1667 s ≈ 166.7 ms
d_s = 550 + 17,000 + 550 = 18,100 km
RTT_s = 2 × 18,100 km / 299,792 km/s
RTT_s ≈ 0.1208 s ≈ 120.8 ms
where
RTT: the propagation round-trip time
d: the one-way path length, in kilometres (km)
v: the propagation speed, in kilometres per second (km/s)
RTT_f: the fibre path's round trip; light in fibre travels at c / n, where c (the vacuum speed of light) is 299,792 km/s and n (the assumed effective group index for signal delay) is 1.47, giving 203,940 km/s
d_s: the one-way length of the space route
RTT_s: the space route's round trip at the vacuum speed of light
km/s: kilometres per second
s: second
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the space route is about 6% longer but light goes about 47% faster in vacuum than in glass, so it wins by about 46 ms.
```

These follow from the supplied fictional path lengths; they are not measured London–Sydney routes. An orbital arc, slant range, inter-satellite hop geometry, ground routing and processing can change the comparison. No actual service advantage is guaranteed.
